So, I was also skeptical of the aids, as I have been wearing aids for 35 years.  You get comfortable with aids, and your brain works hard to compensate - you don't realize how hard until there is a change (good or bad).  So, I went in and got a pair.  Not that I have $7K to throw around, but if I heard just 10% better, then that is an ROI that I can justify.  

I traveled from San Diego to NY to see my daughter, so I made an appointment.  I told myself that I could return them, so I didn't feel the $7K was at risk.   
  
I kept the aids due to their noise-cancellation and speech-focus in AI mode.  And I could tell that my brain-body was better, as I didn't even notice that my aids were in.  I also kept the aids, as my 10% did get better at Fortell's forte: hearing conversations in loud bars and restaurants.  They are way better than my Oticon aids (that cost me about the same).

If you are a hearing aid user, you know that correcting hearing loss is more of an art than a science, given the changing nature of hearing loss (dB changes across frequencies).  I feel Fortell is making it more of a science.  Their service model is basically remote for me, and to my surprise, it has worked out fine.  

I suggest writing down your top 10 problems and what would satisfy you in the hunt for new aids.  It sounds like proven studies between hearing aid manufacturers is a top priority.  Good luck in your journey.

For me, I don't think there was one dramatic moment where I suddenly realized I couldn't hear anymore.

It was more like a bunch of little things that kept happening.

I'd ask people to repeat themselves, especially if there was background noise.

I'd find myself watching someone's face while they were talking because I was trying to fill in the words I didn't catch.

I'd turn the TV up and then realize it was probably louder than everyone else wanted it to be.

And sometimes someone would say something, I'd say "what?" and then understand them a second later without them even repeating it.

Looking back, I think that was the point when I started taking my hearing loss more seriously.

I'm curious what it was like for other people？

Recently I’ve started using my hearing aids again after several year of no use. The main reason of me not using them its because the overall hearing loss is not serious enough (for me) to justify use them in daily life. I would have trouble hearing specific people or social situations, but it would never be that much of a hassle (trash excuse to hide the fact that I hate how noisy life gets). Last semester, had a proff which had speech impediment that caused her speech to be very slow and halting. had trouble hearing her throughout the entire semester but somehow managed to pass the class not relaying on lectures but classmates and info online. New semester start, I had to take TWO courses with her, and in one of them it will be hard to hide the fact that I can't hear her, since there are only three of us in total and the interaction will be more one-on-one. Decided to use hearing aids again to check if its helps to any degree. still hadn’t any lectures with her yet, but so far I’ve been using them on my work. One thing Ive noticed so far is i still have trouble trying to understand or make up what ppl are saying. Yes I hear things louder, but it feels that it doesn’t necessarily make speech more clear for me. ive been trying to eavesdrop (lol) some coworkers to test my hearing improvement, but it feels like although I can “hear” the sound they’re making I can’t really make out every word they say, and every time I tried harder to listen every syllable the less I could understand their convo.

Don’t know if im not processing stuff the way im supposed to or my expectations of how hearing aids works are way off. I’ve been thinking maybe im overwhelmed by all the noise that im suddenly hearing and how loud everything is, but I don’t know if you’re capable to get used to it and “adjust” volume levels (as you’re naturally supposed to).

Idk if anyone have any advice on the matter or there are some stuff I should be doing :(

I suggest you do all of these things:

* Get therapy. This is likely urgent, since you do seem to need support and to gett tools for navigating this.

* Meet other Deaf and HoH. Super important for self-esteem and to get practical inspiration for how to do various things and advocating skills.

* Go to an audiologist and get proper help with hearing aids or even CI. You need proper technology. Maybe even RogenOn and Roger table mics for work.

* Learn about your rights, accessibility options at work and get support so you can do your work without too much fatigue.

* Learn sign language - **now**

No wonder you’re exhausted when you try so hard to do things in a hearing way. Your competence isn’t in how much you hear, so be the smart and bright person you are and start looking for more support and for ways that actually enables you to contribute easier.

I never really thought about how different phone calls are until my mom started struggling with hearing loss.
Face-to-face conversations were sometimes manageable because she could see the person talking.
But the phone was completely different.
No facial expressions.
No lip reading.
No way to guess from the situation.
She started letting some calls go to voicemail and asking someone else to listen instead.
After getting hearing aids, one of the things she appreciated most was being able to handle phone calls on her own again.
This made her very excited.
